The Lahontan redside (Richardsonius egregius) is a cyprinid fish endemic to the Lahontan Basin of the western United States, where it occupies a range of lacustrine and riverine habitats. Adult individuals attain a maximum recorded total length of 17 cm [Li = 17 cm], making it one of the larger-bodied members of its genus in the region, though most field-caught specimens are considerably smaller. The species reaches sexual maturity at a total length of 6.2 cm [Lp = 6.2 cm], a size typically achieved during the second growing season in most populations studied. This length corresponds to a standard length of approximately 5.3 cm at first spawning, representing a threshold at which gonadal development is complete and individuals are reproductively viable. Newly hatched larvae emerge from demersal eggs that exhibit a remarkably small wet weight at birth of 0.0009 grams [Wwb = 0.0009 grams], reflecting the minute size of the yolk-dependent embryo immediately after eclosion. This initial mass is derived from the diameter of the fertilised ovum and is consistent with the low maternal investment per offspring typical of broadcast-spawning cyprinids.

The ontogenetic trajectory from the yolksac larva stage to the onset of exogenous feeding is rapid, with mouth opening and first prey capture occurring within the initial days of free-swimming existence. At the other end of the life spectrum, individuals that survive to reproductive senescence achieve a maximum lifespan of roughly 1825 days [am = roughly 1825 days] when maintained under controlled conditions at 16 °C [T = 16 °C], though field records from natural populations suggest that most individuals likely expire considerably earlier due to predation and seasonal environmental stressors. This longevity is consistent with a temperate-zone cyprinid of moderate body size, falling within the range reported for related genera in the Great Basin. The physiological constraints imposed by the relatively cool, oligotrophic waters of the Lahontan system appear to decelerate metabolic processes, contributing to the extended maximum lifespan observed under stable laboratory conditions compared to warmer-water congeners.

Estimates of body mass at key life history transitions provide further insight into the species' allocation strategy during growth and maturation. The ultimate wet weight attained by a fully grown adult, corresponding to the species' asymptotic body mass, is predicted at 57.7 grams [Wwi = 57.7 grams], a value derived from the length-weight regression typical of the species. This mass represents the maximum somatic investment an individual can achieve, though it is rarely realised in wild populations owing to resource limitation and the energetic demands of annual spawning. At the onset of reproductive capability, individuals reach a wet weight at puberty of 2.46 grams [Wwp = 2.46 grams], indicating that the species invests heavily in lengthening growth before allocating substantial resources toward gametogenesis. The ratio of pubertal mass to asymptotic mass, approximately 4.3 percent, suggests a life history that prioritises early attainment of a threshold body size before diverting energy to reproduction.

The ecological context of the Lahontan redside in its native drainage provides a framework for interpreting these metrics. The species is iteroparous and exhibits a protracted spawning season during the spring and early summer, when water temperatures rise above a critical threshold. Field surveys confirm that adults can survive up to 1825 days [am = up to 1825 days] at 16 °C [T = 16 °C], a temporal window that accommodates repeated annual spawning bouts over several seasons. The record size of 17 cm [Li = 17 cm] observed among the oldest specimens reflects the species' capacity for indeterminate growth, allowing continued increase in body length well after the onset of reproduction. In comparison, sympatric cyprinids of similar body plan often display shorter observed longevities and smaller maximum sizes, suggesting that the Lahontan redside occupies a relatively slow-paced life history niche within the assemblage.

An additional perspective on the species' reproductive biology is gained by examining the mass of offspring at the initiation of independent life. Neonatal mass in this species is a mere 0.0009 grams [Wwb = 0.0009 grams], placing the tiny yolksac larvae among the smallest propagules produced by Great Basin cyprinids. This minimal investment per offspring is counterbalanced by the production of numerous small eggs during each spawning event, a strategy well suited to the pelagic larval phase that follows. The body length marking the transition to sexual maturity is 6.2 cm [Lp = 6.2 cm], which together with the corresponding pubertal mass of 2.46 grams [Wwp = 2.46 grams] defines a consistent reproductive threshold, beyond which individuals can channel surplus energy into annual gamete production. Captive cohorts maintained in aquaria at 16 °C [T = 16 °C] have been observed to live as long as 1825 days [am = 1825 days], confirming that in the absence of predation and with ad libitum feeding, the species can achieve the upper bounds predicted by growth-based longevity estimates.
